newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Chinese premier has talks with Brazil's Cardoso.
newsitem.headline: Chinese premier has talks with Brazil's Cardoso.

text.p: Chinese Premier Li Peng met Brazilian President Fernando Henrique Cardoso in Brasilia on Friday for talks on trade issues and political ties, officials said.
A Presidential Palace official said the 90-minute talks focused on cooperation in satellite technology, agriculture, hydroelectric projects and mining.
"The issue of human rights was also touched on but very briefly," the official said, requesting anonymity.
Li's four-day official visit to Brazil, the second leg of a three-nation Latin American tour, will take him to the industrial metropolis of Sao Paulo on Saturday and the Amazon rain forest on Monday.

After their talks, Cardoso and Li presided over the signing of three accords: one on further satellite cooperation, another on the environment and a third allowing Brazil to maintain its consulate in Hong Kong after the British colony is handed back to Beijing next July 1.

Vera Machado, director general of the Brazilian Foreign Ministry's Asia and Oceania department, told Reuters joint satellite research and commercial development was the most important element of bilateral relations.
China and Brazil have established a $150 million joint venture to produce earth-monitoring satellites, the first of which is scheduled to be launched next October.
The new accord, signed Friday in Brasilia, will allow other "peaceful" uses of future Chinese-Brazilian satellites.
The Presidency official said much of Cardoso and Li's meeting was taken up with the desire to improve commerce.
"They both agreed that trade between our two countries is small and should be much greater," he said.

Bilateral trade totalled $2.243 billion in 1995, sharply up from $1.286 billion the year before. But Brazilian officials said these figures were insignificant in relation to the size of the two countries and their economies.
On Saturday, Li was due to visit the Brazilian government's agricultural research agency, EMBRAPA, just outside the capital.
Officials say Beijing is interested in buying up soybean plantations in Brazil in exchange for Chinese agro-technology, but so far no formal proposals have been made.

It was unclear whether Li broached recent Brazilian moves to stem imports from China such as placing quotas on textiles, punitive tariffs on toys and a 288 percent tariff on pencil imports. But officials on both sides have said no acrimony was expected.
Li, who came from Chile, travels to Venezuela next Tuesday.
